changedBeliefs: Growing `decodeQuery`'s `List<Object?>` is not amortised-free, and it is the single largest Dart-side cost of a large read. A standalone AOT reproduction of the decode loop over a fixed cell buffer measures 2318 us for the doubling path against 865 us pre-sized on 10k x 20 INTEGER, with loads + switch + stores together under 500 us. That lands within 8% of exp 251's 2524 us of `Dart result construction` on the same shape, so the bucket exp 251 refused to design against is mostly buffer growth rather than cell decoding. Growth costs what it costs because a `List<Object?>` grow copies every live element with a store barrier into a freshly faulted array; a 200k-slot result copies ~322k slots through ~5 MB of transient garbage.

Exp 059 rejected this mechanism for the wrong reason and with a design defect. Its stated grounds were the April release suite's noise floor and medians taken across iterations; its mechanism claim (`list growth is already cheap`, `only ~3-4 growths`) counts growths rather than slots copied and is false; and it sized the *initial* allocation from the hint, which is precisely the change exp 067 measured as a 40-44% regression on small-query workloads the same day. A win on large reads and a regression on small ones nets to the noise it reported.

A per-isolate cache is not a durable place for anything a large read teaches. Results over `sacrificeSlotThreshold` (32768 slots) return via `Isolate.exit` and end the worker that produced them, so a hint kept in the worker's schema cache is discarded exactly when the result was large enough to need it, and otherwise describes only the executions that landed on one of four pool workers. Measured directly: the worker-local version won 30-35% on sub-threshold reads and ~1% on the 200k-slot lane. Moving the memory to `ReaderPool` and stamping it on the request took the same lane to -25%.

A size hint must be applied where a wrong answer cannot cost anything. Applied to the initial allocation, a hint saturated by a `SELECT ... LIMIT ?` statement's large leg made its 50-row leg 2.8x slower (68 -> 198 us) — zero-filling 60000 unused slots costs more than the doubling it removes. Applied at the growth step the same lane is neutral by construction, because a result that fits in the initial buffer never reaches the code. This is a stronger guarantee than a floor: it makes the whole mechanism unreachable for small results rather than merely conservative.

Per-request bookkeeping on the main isolate is measurable on a point read. The first version's two map lookups per request cost ~0.3 us, about 6% of a point query, attributed by building a variant with the pool bookkeeping removed and watching the lane return to baseline. Reading the entry once per request and never creating one for a SQL that has not exceeded the initial buffer brought it under the 3% effect floor.

claims.text: Sizing `decodeQuery`'s result buffer from a main-isolate memory of what the same SQL returned before — applied at the first growth, never to the initial allocation — is worth a reproduced -25.1% / -24.8% on 10k x 20 INTEGER, -32.2% / -33.7% on 5k x 4 INTEGER, and -33.6% / -32.3% on the repo's canonical 6-column product row at 10k rows (3.5 ms -> 2.3 ms), measured end to end through the public `select()`. Both controls (200-row and point reads, which never reach the growth path) move opposite signs inside the 3% floor, and both mispredict guards are neutral.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · cross-worktree A/B · two order-flipped passes · 31 samples/lane · 2026-08

claims.text: Buffer growth, not cell decoding, is most of the Dart-side cost of a large read. Reproducing the decode loop over a fixed cell buffer at 10k x 20 INTEGER: doubling from the 256-row initial allocation 2318 us, pre-sized 865 us, loads + switch with no list store 331 us, and `List.filled(200000, null)` alone 405 us. Exp 251's 2524 us for the same shape's `Dart result construction` is therefore a growth measurement more than a decode one.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT standalone microbenchmark · 40 reps · 2026-08

claims.text: A worker-local cache cannot hold anything learned from a large result. `Isolate.exit` on a result over `sacrificeSlotThreshold` ends the worker, so a size hint kept in the per-worker schema cache won 30-35% on sub-threshold reads and ~1% on the 200k-slot lane; the same hint carried on the request from the main isolate won -25% there.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · focused A/B, both hint placements against one baseline · 2026-08

claims.text: Pre-sizing from a converged row hint lowers total bytes allocated per query by 14-61% (the doubling sequence's intermediate arrays stop existing) but does NOT uniformly lower peak buffer capacity. Doubling's overshoot is 1x-2x depending on where the result falls relative to a power-of-two boundary; a converged hint's is always 1.25x. Peak capacity is 23.7% smaller for a result that overshoots a boundary (all three primary lanes) and 22-25% LARGER for one that lands just under it (mixed6-1k, and 2048 rows x 6 columns). Arithmetic on the allocation path only — no RSS or heap sampling was taken, so a workload sensitive to peak rather than churn needs its own measurement.
claims.conditions: derived from the growth path, not measured · 2026-08

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/select_rows_presize.dart` is the durable gate for any change to the result buffer's allocation or growth. Keep its two sub-initial-buffer control lanes (`mixed6-200`, `point1`) — they are inert by construction, so their delta reads the per-binary layout offset directly — and both mispredict guards, which are the only lanes that can expose a size hint's failure mode.

The remaining Dart-side per-cell work in `decodeQuery` is now genuinely the loads, the switch and the stores: ~500 us for 200k INTEGER cells, or ~2.5 ns/cell. Exp 251's decomposition should be read through claim 260.2 before anything else is designed against its `Dart result construction` figure — most of that number was growth, and it is gone.

The same question applies to every other buffer that grows by doubling on a hot path: `selectBytes`'s native `json_buf` already persists and grows geometrically, and the writer's parameter arena is sized per call. Neither has been measured for growth-copy cost the way the row buffer now has.

Anything a worker learns and wants to keep has to live on the main isolate or be re-derivable, because the sacrifice path destroys reader isolates on exactly the largest results. The schema cache itself has this shape — it is rebuilt from `sqlite3_column_name` after every sacrifice — and has never been measured.
